Presidential RamblingsBy Steve Hansen
I see little buds poking up in the flower bed – yay!
With renewal in mind the Guild is beginning to
plan on going beyond Turning 101 and offer some
workshops on many of the other skills that we use
in our shops or studios. The topics being considered are sharpening, sanding, threading, managing wood, finishing, hollowing, and so on. Please
stay
tuned
as
we
recruit
facilitators/
demonstrators and space to lead these workshops.
I have been keeping an eye on Forest Innovation
Investment, https://www.bcfii.ca/about/ and The
Wood Innovation Group, https://twigbc.ca/ both
British Columbia based organizations that focus
on adding value to B.C.’s forest products through
innovation and cooperation among industry players. The reason I bring this up is that they advocate the harvest from our 2nd and 3rd growth
timber stands and they advocate secondary industry as opposed to exporting raw logs. As an adjunct it also occurs to me that so many of these
smaller companies might be approachable as a
way to gain access to wood that is otherwise difficult to get. There is a registry of members on the
FII site. Maybe here’s an opportunity to tap into
that.
One last word on the Tea Pots Challenge for next
month - I’m revising it so that those that find it a
daunting task to make a tea pot can instead make
a tea cup. I am thinking in the Asian tradition of a
handleless cup, but the door is always open for
your own interpretation – that’s what makes it
fun.
Steve

Editor’s NotesBy Steve Fairbairn
Happy New Year and Gung Hay Fat Choy! I hope
everyone had a happy and restful holiday season
and, hopefully some quality time in your workshops/studios.
We kick off the New Year with another installment of our Guild Member Profiles. This month
we are featuring Bruce Campbell. Bruce is also a
consistently prolific contributor to our newsletter
and my predecessor as newsletter editor.
As well as his monthly Tech Talk summary article,
Bruce has also contributed an excellent and detailed follow-up tutorial to his guild demonstration of turning shaftless peppermills that he presented at our last monthly meeting in November.
Sheila Balzer continues her monthly series documenting her adventures as a new turner and the
guild’s Women In Turning (WIT) representative.
As always, I’m on the hunt for new articles from
our members. Don’t be shy! And don’t worry
about your writing skills, just get it down on paper
- that’s why we have an editor.
Steve
PS - Just kidding about the paper. Please email
your submissions to editor@gvwg.ca

Tech TalkBy Bruce Campbell
The last Tech Talk ZOOM session of 2022 was held
at 7:00PM on Monday November 28th, 2022. We
were all starting to think about the holiday season
and many of us were in the shop tidying up the last
bits of our handmade gifts. Nonetheless, a number
of us took time to attend the session. As usual, the
discussion was varied and prompted lots of followon thoughts.
Tech Talk will continue to be held via Zoom on the
Monday evening following the Guild meeting. The
credentials for the session are sent to all registered
Guild members and all are encouraged to participate in the free-flowing discussion centered on
technical aspects of woodturning.
Laguna Lathe Laments
I started off the discussion by reporting that my
Laguna REVO1216 was out of commission. As
many chat groups have been reporting, the lathe
gets “stuck” in reverse. Laguna’s fix is to send you
a new switch which, in my case made little difference. BUT, I did make a bad assumption that I
could reverse direction while the lathe was running. This is not the case. Bad things happen.
David confessed to the sin of reading the manual
(gasp!) which say “Don’t do that!” but it would appear that the controller does not have any protection against this happening (like just ignoring you
or stopping). So be warned.
My adventures with buying and swapping digital
displays and controller boards have not yet ended.
After spending $700+ and repeated email exchanges with Laguna my once mighty mini-lathe is still a
boat anchor. I will let everyone know how I resolve
this.
Reversing Directions
My reversing challenges lead to a discussion on the
pros and cons of being about to reverse directions
on-the-fly. For those that own ONEWAY lathes
there is no issue; just turn the knob and the lathe
slows down and then reverses. But for lathes
made in Australia (NOVA and VICMARC) this is not
the case. They just ignore you until you stop the
lathe, throw the switch, and start again. This has
to do with worker safety regulation is Australia and
New Zealand which prohibit “hot switching”.
Gary reports that this is both time-consuming and
annoying but Fraser reminded us that, in some situations, hot-switching can be dangerous.
As a ONEWAY owner I find myself switching directions all the time whether in sanding (most often)
or to make a clean push cut in a tight place. Like
anything, we get used to what we have and I use
this feature of my lathe all the time. I just wish my
Laguna did it too.
All about the Spindle Roughing Gouge (SRG)
Keith reported that he was unhappy with the finish
he was getting using his SRG and asked about
sharpening and usage. Two factors will influence
the cut of a SRG – how it is sharpened and how it is
presented to the work. For sharpening here are
some guidelines:
Strive to grind the cutting edge 90 degrees to the
shaft of the tool. This makes the tool perform the
same no matter how much it is rolled to the right
or left;
When roughing present the tool perpendicular to
the work;
A SRG is a very versatile tool that can do a number
of different jobs. Of course, its main purpose is to
make no-round timbers round (dah!), but it can do
more. When one wing is presented to the work it
can cut very nearly as well as a skew. When held
with the flute fully closed it can make a clean

plunge cut on the end of a piece. By rolling a little
past vertical it can cut a nice, clean dovetail tenon
and using the same technique as a bowl gouge, it
can act the same way – BUT NEVER ON THE INSIDE
OF A BOWL
Perhaps the most common problem is maintaining
a proper bevel angle. Because the tool is to large it
can be hard to know that you have raised the handle too much and your tool is beginning to scrape
rather than cut.
With practice, a large spindle gouge can do very
fine work. Some pen turners have found they can
do almost all of their pre-sanding cuts with a large
SRG.
More information on sharping a SRG can be found
in on page 5 of our January 2022 newsletter
https://gvwg.ca/docs/Newsletter2022/
January2022.pdf
Keeping the Figure
Brian made several rolling pins for gifts this year
and wanted suggestions to make the figure “pop”
and then keep it that way. The first factor is that
any finish should be food safe but the finish cannot
interfere with the way a rolling pin is used. I suggested that a sealing kind of finish like Wipe-onPoly would likely be too sticky when rolling dough
and if any moisture got under the finish it would
likely blemish to finish.
After talking it around we seemed to agree that the
tried-and-true oil finish would be best both in
terms of use and for ease of care for the lucky recipients.
About Steb Centers
Steb centers are a unique kind of drive spur featuring a spring-loaded center pin surrounded by a ring
of sharp points. They come in several sizes and can
have Morse Tapers mounts or be designed to be
held in a 4-jaw chuck. There even is a version that
works as a live center.
The main advantage of these drives comes when
working hard timbers such as cocobolo, verawood,
blackwood, boxwood, jatoba, etc. The pin can be
accurately set to a mark and as the tailstock is
tightened the spring is compressed and the points
press in to the wood without having to dig in too
deep.
In the right situation these are a joy to use but they
can be annoying if the wood is too soft (like our
local maple, birch, poplar, or alder). The fibers are
not hard enough to support the torque and the
(Continued from page 4)
(Continued on page 6)
Steb Centres - Morse Taper
Steb Centres - Chuck Mounted
Steb Live Centre

January 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
whole thing can start to spin. Once that happens it
can be difficult to get them to bite again.
Another factor to keep in mind is that the spring
behind the point is constantly “pushing” on the
piece. If you try to cut the work too thin that pressure can warp the work or even crush the fibers as
you try to part off the piece.
Summary: great addition to you shop; the original
Sorby versions are pricey; the clone version are less
costly and work just good; work well in the right
conditions; not so much otherwise.
Finishes
Donna was also working on gifts and wanted information on finishes. I think finishes can be looked
at from several perspectives with the first being
“food safe”. Since 1972 the US Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) considers any finish to be
food safe if it is:
•
a non-drying finish and is certified non-toxic.
This usually means oils like walnut ,mineral, olive, etc.
•
a drying finish and has cured for the time indicated on the product.
Personally, I am more conservative about my finishes and allow 20-23 days for drying finishes and
never on food-contact surfaces. For cutting
boards, rolling pins, and the inside of bowls I use
beeswax products like Clapham’s Salad Bowl Finish.
Hand-rubbed products are applied off-lathe and
can take multiple coats. These can be quite satisfying to use as you retain a close, tactical relationship
with the piece. It does, however, take longer and
require a well-ventilated, dust-free, and temperature controlled environment.
Spray finishes are beautiful when you get them
right but require good equipment, an appropriate
work environment, practiced technique, and excellent maintenance of your gear. Extra things to consider are good PPE, a fume hood (where needed),
water filters on your compressor lines, environmentals like humidity and temperature, and, of
course, a dust-free environment.
On-lathe finishes have the advantage of being less
sensitive to dust and they are quicker to apply.
These include, turner’s polish (there are several
brands out there), paraffin wax applied while the
lathe is moving and then melted in with a burnishing cloth while the lathe is running fast, micro crystalline wax, and shellac-based “French” polishing.
For details on that see page 6 of our June 2011
newsletter found here: https://gvwg.ca/docs/
Newsletter2011/June2011.pdf
Preserving Liquids in the Shop
Our discussion on finishing led to talking about caring of the leftover product in the can/bottle/bag.
Over the years I have encountered lots of suggestions on how to do this. I will share a few but these
all have the same thing in common; removing the
air for the container:
•
Stick you unlit (dah!) propane torch in the can
and turn it on. Run it until you smell propane
and then quickly close the lid. Propane is heavier than air, will push it out of the container and
it will not react with the liquid.
•
For oil-based products, pour water in the container. Being heavier than oil it will sink to the
bottom and raise the level of the product to
eliminate the air. This does require extra work
to be sure the next draw of liquid does not
bring along any water.
•
Drop solid objects in to raise the level top the
top of the can. This is easy to do but is really
messy when the last of the product is use. You
end up with a pile of “finished” solid objects.
•
Use StopLoss bags. These 1 liter plastic bags
are made from plastic that will not react to
most products including Wipe-on-Poly, Tung
Oil, and Emtech (personal experience). Simply
transfer the product from its container into the
bag, squeeze out the air, and put the lid on.
The stand-up design makes them easy to store
on a shelf and it is easy to see how much product you have left. I have keep Tung Oil and
Wipe-on-Poly for years.
(Continued from page 5)
(Continued on page 7)

Scratches After Careful Sanding
Gwenda reported still having scratch marks on her
bowl after sanding carefully to 400 grit. After some
questioning we discovered that she had neglected
to clean the surface after each grit. Even with the
best sandpaper, granules of abrasive can break on
and get mixed in to the dust. If they are not removed they will stay around to scratch the surface
with larger scratches than the finer grit.
Hints for getting a supper sanded finish:
1. Use freshly sharpened tools to make final cuts.
This will eliminate the worst tear-out.
2. Use FEPA sandpaper - one with a P in front of
the grit (e.g. P100); cloth backed; flexible; wet/
dry
3. Start with the right grit. If the surface is not
smooth start at 80 or 100
4. Use the 50% rule. The next grit should be no
more that 50% finer than the current grit.
5. Clean the surface with compressed air or a
damp cloth between grits
6. Check for imperfections like blushing or tearout after each grit and go back to the previous
grit to remove them. Spot sanding with a power disk may be required.
7. Reverse directions between grits.
8. Once done, wet the surface with water to raise
the grain. Take a short break (5-10 mins) and
then repeat the last grit. You might want to do
this several times if the grain keeps rising.
Gaining Quill Travel
While not technically a Tech Talk event, David
heard me on a Turner Talk Thursday session talking
about shortening the Morse taper on my Jacobs
Chuck drill setup to give me another ½ inch of quill
travel when I am drilling with the lathe. He had the
same problem so here is what he did:
“When you mentioned that you had your live
center shortened, I thought that was a very
good idea as I had the same problem with
mine. I tried my hacksaw on it (not really
thinking it would work), but it did. The steel is
not very hard, and it took me about a minute
using a cheap bimetal Canadian Tire blade.
“You mentioned that yours wound up a tad
short and you self-ejector no longer works.
Could you turn a wooden insert with a head
on it and cement it to the shortened end?
That would make it a little longer so that it
would have contact and eject when you want
it to.”
Thanks for this, David and I will certain try you suggestion.

Traditional pepper mills are columnar in design
chiefly because of the grinding mechanism. The
shaft is so integral to the mechanism that it requires that the mill be “built” around it. The grinding motion comes from the shaft being twisted and
the fineness of the grind is controlled by a screw
adjustment threaded on to the top of the shaft.
The illustration and picture below shows this nicely:
But, what if you want to break away from this design? What if you do not want a metal knob on the
top or even a columnar design? How can this be
achieved?
In 1994 a unique mechanism was created wherein
the fineness of the grind is adjusted by a knob on
the bottom of the mechanism. This eliminated the
need to a knob on the top but it still had a shaft
that needed to fit in to some cranking mechanism
– usually a cap of the top of the piece. They also
designed a version that dispensed with the shaft
for the cranking and moved it to the top of the
cranking mechanism itself; named the “shaftless”
CrushGrind.
I took up the challenge to create pepper mills that
(Continued on page 10)
Re
-imagining the Pepper MillBy Bruce Campbell
CrushGrind Mechanisms

January 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
did not have the traditional columnar design and
for that I chose the shaft-less CrushGrind mechanism. First I had to figure out how to use them
with little information available. However, I did
find a diagram on the Net and, after converting it
from metric to inches, started there.
Installing a Shaft-less CrushGrind Mechanism
The way the shaft-less mechanism works is that the
lower half is press-fitted into the lower section of a
mill with about half of it projecting above. Then a
matching section is pressed over the top half so it
“locks” in place using three flexible clips that fit into a groove.
This is a little challenging as the groove must be
accurately placed; too high and the clips will not
engage; too low and the top will not seat with the
bottom. Fortunately, the procedure I developed
allows this to be easily checked and corrected.
Choosing the drill bits:
There are six “ribs” on the lower part of the mechanism and six on the upper part. As the mechanism
is pressed in a drilled hole, these ribs are designed
to dig in to the wood and prevent the body of the
mechanism from rotating while the internals do
the grinding. If the wood is too hard these ribs will
get sheared off and prevent the mechanism from
setting in properly. Such woods would include
hard maple, cocobolo, blackwood, boxwood, etc.
To prevent this, a slightly larger drill should be
used. Alternately, if the wood is soft (such as well
spalted woods) a smaller drill should be used so
the ribs have more timber in which to bite. The diagram shows the largest and smallest drills that can
be used before they exceed the limits of the mechanism.
I have been successful using Big Leaf Maple, Walnut, and Cherry with 1 ¾”, 1 ½”, and 1” Forstner
bits. I have an inexpensive set of bits but I took the
time to sharpen and balance the cutting edges before I started (see Tech Talk in the October 2021
Guild newsletter for more details: https://gvwg.ca/
docs/Newsletter2021/October2021.pdf )
Drilling Procedure:
Please refer to the drilling diagram while reviewing
this procedure:
•
choose a straight-grain blank at least 3” long x
2 ½” square
•
mount the blank between centers
•
turn round to no less than 2 ¼” dia or leave as
is (i.e., a whole branch)
•
cut a tenon on the “top” end and mount the
blank in a 4-jaw chuck
•
Using the 1 ¾” bit drill a hole at least 5/8”
deep. This is to ensure the grey adjusting knob
does not protrude beyond the base.
•
Using the 1 ½” bit drill 1 7/16” + the kerf of
your parting tool or saw. If you prefer you can
adjust for the kerf later.
•
Using a thin parting tool part the lower part of
the wood off about 1 ¼” from the bottom
(Continued from page 9)
(Continued on page 11)
Drilling Diagram

January 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 11
•
Completely sand and finish both sides of the
part; this cannot be done once the pieces are
assembled. Also sand the top part of the 1 ¼”
hole. This will make it a little bit larger and help
to prevent binding if the timber moves once
assembled.
•
Insert the mechanism into the lower section. It
is best to set up a simple stand that supports
the piece bottom-up without blocking the
drilled hole. Allow for about 2” of clearance
below to allow the mechanism to project far
enough. The mechanism can be pressed in by
hand or a simple “pusher” can be made if more
force is required. Be sure the mechanism is
pressed firmly in place.
•
Measure how far the mechanism protrudes beyond the wood to the large shoulder and compare that to the depth of the hole in in the section that is still in the chuck. These should be
the same. If the hole is too shallow use the 1
½” bit to drill it a bit deeper. Strive to get the
hole about 1/32” deeper than the protruding
section of the mechanism. If the hole is already
deeper then carefully trim the lip until the correct depth is achieved.
•
Using the 1” bit, drill a minimum of ¾” beyond
the bottom of the 1 ½” hole. This can be deeper if you wish and any extra length will serve as
a reservoir for pepper corns or salt crystals.
•
Cut a groove at least 1/8” deep x ¼” high with
the lower edge EXACTLY 3/8” up the 1” hole.
Done correctly, this ensures that the clips on
the top of the mechanism will engage and hold
the top and bottom together
•
Finally, using the same push stick as before,
press the bottom section firmly in to the top.
•
DONE!
Cutting the groove requires a special cutter. I
made one from an old planer blade while others
have modified a hollowing tool or cut down and
sharpen a 3/8” Allen key. For some ideas on how
to do this go to the Tech Talk column on page 5 of
the October 2022 Guild newsletter (https://
gvwg.ca/docs/Newsletter2022/October2022.pdf ).
Below is the drawing I made up my cutter and a
picture of it.
Ready to Innovate
By following the procedures above one gets a
“cartridge” that can be mounted in anything large
enough to accommodate it. So how can this be
used to “innovate”? First, consider the basic elements required in a grinder:
•
gravity – users expect the pepper to fall out of
(Continued from page 10)
(Continued on page 12)
Notch Cutter
Notch Cutter Dimensions

the mechanism but not necessarily straight
down
•
a grinding mechanism – in our case the shaftless CrushGrind mechanism
•
a way to twist the mechanism – the way the
mechanism is pressed in the top and bottom
parts as detailed above provides the way to
twist. However, it imposes a requirement that
the body be in two parts and the joint needs to
be perpendicular to the mechanism.
•
a reservoir for the salt, pepper, coriander, etc.
– The reservoir need not be large. One or two
tablespoons is enough for over 100 “average”
uses.
•
a way to fill the reservoir – fortunately, the
grinder on the CrushGrind can be removed by
unthreading the grey adjusting nut on the
bottom. Once it is removed there is room to fill
the reservoir.
As long as the design addresses these conditions
we can now let our imaginations go “wild”. Here
are unique ways that a mill can be configured:

Guild Member Profile
- Bruce Campbell
By Bruce Campbell with Diana Dougherty
Tell us about your background – how did you
get into woodturning?
I began woodturning in 1979 when I found a homebuilt wood lathe in the crawl space of an old garage. I made a stand for it and used a 1/3 HP washing machine motor to drive it. Knowing no better, I
used my bench chisels as scrapers and “started
turning”. I still have my very first project – a pair of
candlesticks.
There were very few books on woodturning back
then but I picked up small tips here and there and
learned by trial and error – mostly error. I moved
to the US in 1980 and gave that lathe to a friend. I
returned to Canada in 1982 and over the next few
years bought several basic commercial lathes and
outgrew them as my skill grew and I took on bigger
projects. The real change came in 1995 through an
unexpected email inviting me to attend a weeklong seminar with Richard Rafffan. That week
transformed me as a turner. I wrote later, “What
before was hard became easier and what seemed
impossible became doable.” I outgrew my 16”
lathe soon after and purchased my current one; a
ONEWAY 2436.
In 1998 I had a brief conversation with local bowl
turner John Beese who talked about a university
professor who wanted to form a woodturning club.
Some months later I became part of a small group
lead by that professor; Art Liestman and through
his vision I became part of the formation of the
GVWG. The activities of the Guild have pushed,
pulled, taught and inspired me beyond anything I
would have accomplished on my own and continues to do so today. For that guidance and fellowship I am immensely grateful.
Tell us about your workshop/studio.
Oh, my. My studio is not the smallest in the Guild
but it is what real estate agents call a “Step Saver”.
I work in an unheated 1-car enclosed carport. I
have the ONEWAY lathe, an 18” Laguna bandsaw, a
benchtop drill press, a half speed grinder with 80
and 180 CBN wheels and a 32 slot tool rack above
it. A steel cabinet/drawer unit, two benches and a
few shelves fill up the rest of the space with little
room for much else. Yet, somehow, there always
seems to be extra “stuff” all over the place. AKA, it
is a mess.
(Continued on page 15)
Bruce Campbell
First Turnings 1979 -Candle Sticks - 3X4” - Apple

January 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 15
What tools do you most like using on your
lathe?
I have been doing commercial turning since 2002
and almost all of that has been spindle work. As a
result I do about 90% of my turning with a 1 ¼” or
2” spindle rouging gouge. Nonetheless, I do use all
32 tools in my tool rack. If not, I get rid of them.
I think the most important thing about tools is to
buy good ones made by reputable makes. Tools
last a long time, even cheap ones. So it is important to have tools that will grow with you as
your skills improve.
What is your favorite wood?
There are several exotics that are a real joy to turn.
They include blackwood, cocobolo, boxwood, verawood and lignum vitae. But rather than fixating on
any one species, I really enjoy trying to bring out
the beauty and strength from any timber. While I
mostly work with hardwoods some so called softwood are a joy as well. Old growth timbers, rare
species, and those that grow near our mountainous timberline can be quite magical.
I avoid spalted wood as I tend to get congested
when working it and I don’t turn red cedar if I can
help it or yellow cedar ever. I am also quite allergic
to Purple Rhododendron (contact rash in minutes)
and Greenheart (instant coughing).
What finishes do you prefer using?
I prefer to apply finishes on-the-lathe so my common finish is a beeswax/oil paste. When making
bowls I use a modified French polish technique using rattle-can lacquer and mineral oil on the outside. I find it withstands being handled with wet
hands quite well. But on the inside I prefer a finish
that the owner can refresh easily. For me that is a
beeswax/oil product – in my case Clapham’s Salad
Bowl Finish.
Off-lathe finishing is not really my strong suit as I
am just not as patient as I need to be and I do not
have a proper finishing space. I very much like

In many ways my martial arts training informs and
parallels my woodturning. Martial arts are about
refining one’s self physically, mentally, spiritually
and emotionally. I approach my woodturning the
same way. I am constantly looking for ways to improve me physical turning skills and thinking about
woodturning techniques and methods. I also use
the making process to explore emotional issues
and to strive to uplift and inspire both myself and
those around me.
What inspires you – where do you get your
ideas from?
This is a favorite topic for me as many people I
meet feel they have no talent or useful ideas. I
think that is rubbish. We all have physical abilities
and personal preferences. What we lack is practice
and a safe place to express ourselves. That is one
of the great things the Guild gives us – a venue to
learn, practice, and share. Arthur C. Clarke once
wrote that sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic. I have a similar
thought that with sufficiently advanced skill is indistinguishable from talent.
If people feel they are “stuck” I encourage them to
pick a piece they like and copy it 10 times. I assure
you that by the 7th or 8th time you will have ideas
about what else you could do along these lines. So
do that and get new ideas and do them and so on
and so on.
I have the great good luck to be married to a brilliant crafter and artist who paints, does leatherwork, gardens, does silver work, sews, draws,
cooks, and is constantly “doing”. That constant
creative energy gives me a steady stream of ideas
and inspirations.
Our Guild serves a similar role through our regular
presentations, our Instant Galleries, the President’s
Challenge, Tech Talk, Wood Chats, our newsletters,
and our incredible web site. If you ever feel
“stuck” for ideas just plug in to any of them and
your brain will light up.
Who has been the greatest influence on your
work?
For technique, Richard Raffan, Stuart Batty, and
Don Derry all came into my life at just the time
when I was ready to absorb what they had to say.
Creatively, the list is really long. Many on that list
were turners who visited the Guild to give demos
and teach classes. Spiritually, another long list of
martial arts instructors have guided me and emotionally, I give full credit to my wife, Shirley.

work?
Most of my work is sold before it is made. That is,
it is ordered by a customer. I sell several hundred

lot of my shop time.
I find gallery sales to be time-consuming and not
very profitable. As a result, I only sell in one small
gallery shop with whom I have a long relationship

I think we define ourselves, at least partly, by the
things we do; the parent/lawyer/soccer coach or

parts of our life changes or disappears we are

things, or course, but those four things define me
and I plan to do them for the remainder of my life.

Safety Guidelines for WoodturningYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 33)

January 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 33
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage.
